news.headline: ‘Preserve amputated leg of chainsaw attack accused’: Andhra Pradesh HC orders hospital
news.story_lead: ‘Preserve amputated leg of chainsaw attack accused’: Andhra Pradesh HC orders hospital The high court passed the order on Tuesday on a petition that sought a CBI probe into the police firing at the alleged chainsaw attacker The Andhra Pradesh High Court has directed the Anantapur Government General Hospital to preserve the amputated right leg of Hemanth alias Dummu, the 21-year-old accused in the chainsaw attack on a Class 10 schoolgirl in Raptadu on October 31. A bench of chief justice Lisa Gill and justice Challa Gunaranjan passed the order on Tuesday on a petition that sought a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the police firing at the accused, Hemanth alias Dummu. The high court told hospital superintendent Dr D Malleswari and the police to take necessary steps to preserve the amputated limb.
news.full_article_text: ‘Preserve amputated leg of chainsaw attack accused’: Andhra Pradesh HC orders hospital The high court passed the order on Tuesday on a petition that sought a CBI probe into the police firing at the alleged chainsaw attacker The Andhra Pradesh High Court has directed the Anantapur Government General Hospital to preserve the amputated right leg of Hemanth alias Dummu, the 21-year-old accused in the chainsaw attack on a Class 10 schoolgirl in Raptadu on October 31. A bench of chief justice Lisa Gill and justice Challa Gunaranjan passed the order on Tuesday on a petition that sought a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the police firing at the accused, Hemanth alias Dummu. The high court told hospital superintendent Dr D Malleswari and the police to take necessary steps to preserve the amputated limb. The bench also told the government to file counter affidavits on the application and adjourned the case to December 30. Hemanth was picked up in the district’s Atmakur forest on November 1, a day after he allegedly attacked the schoolgirl with the chainsaw. She survived the attack and is being treated at Manipal Hospital in Bengaluru . According to the police, Hemanth allegedly tried to escape when he was being taken to reconstruct the crime scene and hurled stones at police personnel, injuring them. The police personnel subsequently opened fire at the suspect, who sustained injuries to his leg. Mangalagiri-based advocate Gunda Gopikrishna filed the petition on November 2. The following day, doctors at Anantapur’s district hospital amputated Hemanth’s right leg after gangrene set in from damaged blood vessels. During proceedings on Tuesday, special government pleader S Pranathi told the court that the accused was in judicial custody and undergoing treatment at the hospital. Also Read: Andhra youth, who attacked schoolgirl with chainsaw, injured in police firing during ‘escape attempt’ She said the amputated limb would undergo standard forensic testing and the relevant assessment would be shared with the bench. An application filed by the petitioner to implead education department officials, however, was rejected by the court, which questioned whether there was a link between the relief sought in the petition and the education department Doctors indicated that Hemanth was also suffering from severe drug withdrawal symptoms. Medical superintendent Dr D Malleswari said Hemanth suffered a sudden drop in pulse rate and fell from his bed earlier this week, requiring emergency medical intervention. Dr Malleswari said individuals who have become dependent on narcotic substances may experience severe physical and psychological reactions when they suddenly stop consuming them. “Such withdrawal symptoms can include fluctuations in blood pressure, an unusually rapid or slow heartbeat, mental instability, insomnia, anxiety and digestive disorders,” she said.

news.full_article_text: US midterms have opened the door to global climate cooperation Navtej SarnaOn the landscape of our discontent, several craters pose immediate challenges: Conflicts without end, struggling multilateral institutions, trade handcuffed by tariffs, the looming AI takeover, and so on On the landscape of our discontent, several craters pose immediate challenges: Conflicts without end, struggling multilateral institutions, trade handcuffed by tariffs, the looming AI takeover, and so on. It is easy, and often profitable, to turn one’s face away from the challenge of climate change. Performative grandstanding – as we will no doubt see at COP 31 in Antalya, Turkey — or superficial greenwashing is considered sufficient. This deliberate downplaying or ignoring of the climate crisis now has a name: Climate hushing. But monsters don’t go away with a finger on their lips. While the world is looking elsewhere, the Earth’s climate system is hurtling headlong into uncharted waters. Several vital markers of the climate crisis are at record extremes: Carbon dioxide levels are higher now than at any time in the last two million years; extreme heat, droughts, floods and wildfires are common occurrences; glacier thickness and Greenland ice mass are at record lows. Staying below the 2015 Paris goal of 1.5 degree Celsius warming is no longer possible. Further, the climate crisis is intersecting with biodiversity loss, freshwater stress, food shortages, pathogens and geopolitical instability. Most of these trends are anthropogenic, driven by unsustainable human activity, particularly fossil fuel dependence. The consequences are inequitable in the extreme: while the rich grow richer, Global South communities and the small island States, historically the least responsible for emissions, bear the most severe consequences. Yet the gap between climate science and societal response continues to widen, even as the risks escalate. The US under President Donald Trump has been particularly culpable. Trump believes climate change is a hoax and a conspiracy by China to make US manufacturing uncompetitive. He has withdrawn twice from the 2015 Paris Agreement, saying “I was elected to represent the citizens of Pittsburgh, not Paris.” By early 2027, the US will have withdrawn from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Intergovernmental Panel of Climate Change (IPCC), the leading authority on climate science. The absence from these forums of the world’s largest economy and historically the largest contributor to greenhouse gas accumulation weakens the already fragile international climate cooperation; other countries find it easier to blunt their own climate ambitions. International climate financing and technological assistance for mitigation, adaptation and energy transformation all lose steam. Trump’s policies have expanded fossil-fuel production (represented by the slogan, Drill, baby, drill) while exposing, through his misguided war on Iran, the deep vulnerabilities of a fossil-fuel based global economy. He has reversed and defunded Biden-era clean energy initiatives, rolled back regulatory constraints protecting the environment and forests, and stopped offshore wind projects. In the process, he has handed over the central position in solar manufacturing, battery supply chains and several clean-energy technologies to China. The dramatic results of the recent midterm polls present a slim hope for the repair of the US’s climate policies, with both domestic and international impact. While climate was not on the ballot – Democratic candidates were advised to practise climate hushing -- climate policy was very much there by implication: A war that exposed the vulnerability of fossil fuel dependence, rising energy costs, climate disasters and wildfires, and the acne-like breakout of data centres across the country made up the affordability crisis that agitated the voters. Climate-forward Democrats have won the first round against oil companies, Big Tech and Big Money but it remains to be seen how effectively they can mend specific climate policies. While Trump’s veto powers will hamper major legislative changes, Democrats are likely to exercise greater budgetary oversight, resist further deregulation and encourage clean energy investments. Fully reversing many of Trump’s acts may have to await a change in the Oval Office or a significant bipartisan consensus. Opposition to data centres is one issue that has bipartisan appeal. Data centres are unpopular because of higher energy bills, shrinkage of water resources, noise and air pollution, an increased carbon footprint and a general scepticism towards artificial intelligence. Tougher regulation, or even a moratorium, on data centres could soon be on the cards. State-level climate policies could be another positive development: Several of the newly elected Democratic governors are strong climate advocates: The first female Native American governor Deb Haaland (New Mexico), the first female Black governor Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia), Amy Acton of Ohio and Gina Hinojosa of Texas. Any signal emanating from the US on climate policy will be a welcome impetus to global climate efforts. While there will be no federal delegation from the US at COP 31, the presence of a 19-member delegation of Congressional Democrats at the Conference will send a significant diplomatic message indicating renewed US interest; another large delegation consisting of mayors, governors and a cross-section of representatives at state and city level will also demonstrate engagement at the sub-national level. Once the new US Congress convenes in January 2027, climate and clean energy issues should form a vital part of India’s outreach on the Hill. India has a good story to tell on clean energy, having crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity; renewables are over 50% of installed electricity capacity with solar capacity being the third highest in the world. This story should get a more receptive hearing as climate advocates try to balance out the Trump administration’s focus on energy access and fossil fuel exports from the US. The scaffolding for bilateral cooperation in this field already exists; a more coordinated approach that accelerates technology cooperation and more public as well as private climate finance would assist India’s efforts in generation, manufacturing, storage and transmission of renewable energy. Going beyond the bilateral, India is in a convincing position to play a role as a bridge to the Global South and lead efforts to unblock climate finance and climate technology for developing countries, in particular for adaptation and climate resilience programmes in vulnerable communities. The door to global climate cooperation is once again open, if only by just a crack. Given the existential nature of the threat posed by global warming, the only choice is to push through. It is easy, and often profitable, to turn one’s face away from the challenge of climate change. Performative grandstanding – as we will no doubt see at COP 31 in Antalya, Turkey — or superficial greenwashing is considered sufficient. This deliberate downplaying or ignoring of the climate crisis now has a name: Climate hushing. But monsters don’t go away with a finger on their lips. While the world is looking elsewhere, the Earth’s climate system is hurtling headlong into uncharted waters. Several vital markers of the climate crisis are at record extremes: Carbon dioxide levels are higher now than at any time in the last two million years; extreme heat, droughts, floods and wildfires are common occurrences; glacier thickness and Greenland ice mass are at record lows. Staying below the 2015 Paris goal of 1.5 degree Celsius warming is no longer possible. Further, the climate crisis is intersecting with biodiversity loss, freshwater stress, food shortages, pathogens and geopolitical instability. Most of these trends are anthropogenic, driven by unsustainable human activity, particularly fossil fuel dependence. The consequences are inequitable in the extreme: while the rich grow richer, Global South communities and the small island States, historically the least responsible for emissions, bear the most severe consequences. Yet the gap between climate science and societal response continues to widen, even as the risks escalate. The US under President Donald Trump has been particularly culpable. Trump believes climate change is a hoax and a conspiracy by China to make US manufacturing uncompetitive. He has withdrawn twice from the 2015 Paris Agreement, saying “I was elected to represent the citizens of Pittsburgh, not Paris.” By early 2027, the US will have withdrawn from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Intergovernmental Panel of Climate Change (IPCC), the leading authority on climate science. The absence from these forums of the world’s largest economy and historically the largest contributor to greenhouse gas accumulation weakens the already fragile international climate cooperation; other countries find it easier to blunt their own climate ambitions. International climate financing and technological assistance for mitigation, adaptation and energy transformation all lose steam. Trump’s policies have expanded fossil-fuel production (represented by the slogan, Drill, baby, drill) while exposing, through his misguided war on Iran, the deep vulnerabilities of a fossil-fuel based global economy. He has reversed and defunded Biden-era clean energy initiatives, rolled back regulatory constraints protecting the environment and forests, and stopped offshore wind projects. In the process, he has handed over the central position in solar manufacturing, battery supply chains and several clean-energy technologies to China. The dramatic results of the recent midterm polls present a slim hope for the repair of the US’s climate policies, with both domestic and international impact. While climate was not on the ballot – Democratic candidates were advised to practise climate hushing -- climate policy was very much there by implication: A war that exposed the vulnerability of fossil fuel dependence, rising energy costs, climate disasters and wildfires, and the acne-like breakout of data centres across the country made up the affordability crisis that agitated the voters. Climate-forward Democrats have won the first round against oil companies, Big Tech and Big Money but it remains to be seen how effectively they can mend specific climate policies. While Trump’s veto powers will hamper major legislative changes, Democrats are likely to exercise greater budgetary oversight, resist further deregulation and encourage clean energy investments. Fully reversing many of Trump’s acts may have to await a change in the Oval Office or a significant bipartisan consensus. Opposition to data centres is one issue that has bipartisan appeal. Data centres are unpopular because of higher energy bills, shrinkage of water resources, noise and air pollution, an increased carbon footprint and a general scepticism towards artificial intelligence. Tougher regulation, or even a moratorium, on data centres could soon be on the cards. State-level climate policies could be another positive development: Several of the newly elected Democratic governors are strong climate advocates: The first female Native American governor Deb Haaland (New Mexico), the first female Black governor Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia), Amy Acton of Ohio and Gina Hinojosa of Texas. Any signal emanating from the US on climate policy will be a welcome impetus to global climate efforts. While there will be no federal delegation from the US at COP 31, the presence of a 19-member delegation of Congressional Democrats at the Conference will send a significant diplomatic message indicating renewed US interest; another large delegation consisting of mayors, governors and a cross-section of representatives at state and city level will also demonstrate engagement at the sub-national level. Once the new US Congress convenes in January 2027, climate and clean energy issues should form a vital part of India’s outreach on the Hill. India has a good story to tell on clean energy, having crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity; renewables are over 50% of installed electricity capacity with solar capacity being the third highest in the world. This story should get a more receptive hearing as climate advocates try to balance out the Trump administration’s focus on energy access and fossil fuel exports from the US. The scaffolding for bilateral cooperation in this field already exists; a more coordinated approach that accelerates technology cooperation and more public as well as private climate finance would assist India’s efforts in generation, manufacturing, storage and transmission of renewable energy. Going beyond the bilateral, India is in a convincing position to play a role as a bridge to the Global South and lead efforts to unblock climate finance and climate technology for developing countries, in particular for adaptation and climate resilience programmes in vulnerable communities. The door to global climate cooperation is once again open, if only by just a crack. Given the existential nature of the threat posed by global warming, the only choice is to push through. news.headline: Valid multiple-entry tourist visa doesn’t guarantee entry into India: Delhi high court
news.story_lead: Valid multiple-entry tourist visa doesn’t guarantee entry into India: Delhi high court In her petition, the US national said she was issued a multiple-entry tourist visa on November 28, 2022, that was supposed to be valid until November 27, 2032. A foreign national cannot claim an enforceable right to obtain a visa or enter India solely because they were earlier issued a multiple-entry tourist visa or because that visa is still valid, the Delhi high court has said. In his seven-page order issued on November 5 but released on Tuesday, a bench of justice Amit Mahajan said the issuance of a visa, refusal of entry or granting clearance at immigration is a sovereign function of the State that is embedded in considerations of national security, foreign policy and administrative discretion.
news.full_article_text: Valid multiple-entry tourist visa doesn’t guarantee entry into India: Delhi high court In her petition, the US national said she was issued a multiple-entry tourist visa on November 28, 2022, that was supposed to be valid until November 27, 2032. A foreign national cannot claim an enforceable right to obtain a visa or enter India solely because they were earlier issued a multiple-entry tourist visa or because that visa is still valid, the Delhi high court has said. In his seven-page order issued on November 5 but released on Tuesday, a bench of justice Amit Mahajan said the issuance of a visa, refusal of entry or granting clearance at immigration is a sovereign function of the State that is embedded in considerations of national security, foreign policy and administrative discretion. The Centre is entitled to take into consideration all the relevant factors that may warrant scrutiny, he added. The bench made the remarks while hearing a petition by a US citizen, seeking directions to the Centre to permit her entry into India. “The petitioner, being a foreign national, cannot claim an enforceable right to be granted a visa or to be permitted entry into India merely on the basis that she had earlier been issued a multiple-entry Tourist Visa or that the said visa was stated to be valid until 27.11.2032. The possession of a visa does not, by itself, confer an absolute or unconditional right of admission into India,” it said. In her petition, the US national said she was issued a multiple-entry tourist visa on November 28, 2022, that was supposed to be valid until November 27, 2032. She claimed that during her visits to India, she did not engage in any activity in violation of her visa conditions but during her departure from Chennai airport on January 23, 2024, immigration authorities informed her that her cumulative stay in India in 2023 had exceeded the permissible limit of 180 days. She said that although she paid the prescribed penalty, no order or exit permit was issued to her. When she arrived at Bengaluru airport on November 4, 2024, she was denied entry and orally informed that she could return to India only after April 9, 2026. The petitioner further submitted that she had suffered a fall at her residence in Bali, following which a hospital in Coimbatore had issued an invitation for her to apply for a Medical/AYUSH Visa to receive treatment in India. It added that her application for a 60-day e-Medical/AYUSH Visa to undergo supervised Panchakarma treatment at Vaidyagrama Ayurveda Healing Village in Coimbatore on June 6, was rejected, without any reasons assigned. The court, however, dismissed the plea, saying: “Even otherwise, it is not the function of this Court, in exercise of judicial review, to substitute its own assessment for that of the competent authority in a matter concerning admission of a foreign national.”

Jaiswal’s remarks marked the first acknowledgement from the Indian side about the work on food corridors. The move is also in line with India’s efforts to protect the interests of the countries of the Global South, which have been hit by food, fuel and fertiliser shortages since the start of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Modi and Zelensky shared perspectives on the ongoing conflict during their phone conversation, and discussed its humanitarian aspects and various efforts to restore peace that are currently underway, Jaiswal said. Modi reiterated India’s firm commitment to contribute towards peace in every possible way, and this was followed by the call between Jaishankar and Lavrov that focused on diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the conflict, he said. “India has been emphasising that the way forward is to take the path of dialogue and diplomacy. news.story_lead: Six coaches of Kolkata-Sairang Express derail at Digaru railway station in Assam; rescue ops on Kapinjal Kishore Sharma, CPRO of Northeast Frontier Railway said that there is no report of any casualties so far. Five passenger coaches and the locomotive of the Kolkata–Sairang Express derailed at Digaru railway station on the outskirts of Guwahati in Assam early on Tuesday morning as the pilot lost control while giving precedence to another train. The railway department confirmed that all passengers on the train are safe and no one sustained any injuries in the incident.
news.full_article_text: Six coaches of Kolkata-Sairang Express derail at Digaru railway station in Assam; rescue ops on Kapinjal Kishore Sharma, CPRO of Northeast Frontier Railway said that there is no report of any casualties so far. Five passenger coaches and the locomotive of the Kolkata–Sairang Express derailed at Digaru railway station on the outskirts of Guwahati in Assam early on Tuesday morning as the pilot lost control while giving precedence to another train. The railway department confirmed that all passengers on the train are safe and no one sustained any injuries in the incident. However in a post on X, chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said four people were injured and receiving care. He added that his government was working closely with ministry of railways. “4 sustained minor injuries and are receiving care. We're working closely with @RailMinIndia on this situation. All stranded passengers have been provided with basic necessities and alternative travel train has been arranged for the journey,” he wrote on X. According to the Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR), the incident occurred at Digaru station around 6.54am, when the Kolkata–Sairang Express, coming from Mizoram, derailed after an accident The officials said that six units, including five passenger coaches, derailed as a result of the incident. "The locomotive pilot could not control the speed of the train, resulting in the derailment of the locomotive and five passenger coaches. All passengers are safe and no injuries to anyone," the railway said in a statement, adding that passengers are being transported to their destinations by an alternate train. The NFR said its officials reached the site immediately after the incident and launched the required relief and rescue operations. The General Manager of NFR, along with other railway officials, proceeded to the site. The incident caused delays to several other trains, but no train has been cancelled yet, the NFR said, adding that the Guwahati–Jorhat Town Jan Shatabdi Express and Coimbatore–Silchar Express have been controlled at Panbari and Panikhaiti, respectively. A video surfaced on social media related to the derailment, in which the locomotive pilot can be heard repeatedly saying the brakes were unresponsive, suggesting he couldn't stop the train. news.story_lead: 17-year-old accused in Bengaluru family murders may face adult trial The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults following an assessment The 17-year-old accused of assisting her father in the murder of seven members of their family in Bengaluru could face trial as an adult if a juvenile justice board determines she meets the criteria under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences, including murder, to be tried as adults following a preliminary assessment of their capacity to understand and commit the alleged crime. The girl, a second-year pre-university student at a private college, allegedly assisted S Indushekar, 52, in killing his wife, Sunitha, and six of her relatives at their home over about 15 days in October.

The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences, including murder, to be tried as adults following a preliminary assessment of their capacity to understand and commit the alleged crime. The girl, a second-year pre-university student at a private college, allegedly assisted S Indushekar, 52, in killing his wife, Sunitha, and six of her relatives at their home over about 15 days in October. She was arrested along with her father on November 5. A police officer said investigators are probing the extent of her involvement, including claims by her father that she helped bring relatives to the house, conceal the killings, and transport and dispose of the bodies. “The main point being considered is whether Indushekar manipulated his daughter into helping him dispose of the bodies.” The first information report (FIR) registered in the case on November 5 names Indushekar and his daughter as accused. Indushekar is listed as an adult accused. His daughter is classified as a juvenile in conflict with the law. A juvenile justice board must assess the child’s mental and physical capacity to commit the alleged offence, her ability to understand its consequences, and the circumstances in which it was committed under the Juvenile Justice Act Section 15. The assessment can involve psychologists and other experts. The officer said if the board decides that the case warrants an adult trial, it can transfer the matter to the children’s court under Section 18(3). “The children’s court must independently decide whether the child should face an adult trial or be dealt with under the juvenile justice system.” The officer said the seriousness of the allegations alone does not determine the outcome. The girl’s understanding of the alleged crimes and the extent to which she was influenced or coerced by her father will be important considerations. Investigators suspect that Indushekar turned his daughter against her mother’s family, portraying the relatives as enemies and allegedly telling her that eliminating them would improve their financial position because the property would eventually belong to her. The girl allegedly contacted her maternal grandmother, Roopavathi, after her mother Sunitha’s murder and asked her to visit the house. She allegedly invited her maternal aunts for dinner, telling them that Sunitha was away on a trip. She reportedly messaged her aunt Divya’s sister, Chandana, claiming that the family was travelling. Police are investigating her suspected role in packing the bodies, transporting them in the car, and cleaning the crime scene. Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge said Indushekar allegedly brainwashed his daughter and made her assist in the crime. Police said Indushekar allegedly transported the bodies in his car and disposed of them at different locations with his daughter’s assistance. Forensic Science Laboratory and Scene of Crime Officer teams inspected the recovery sites, while postmortem examinations were conducted. Investigators are now focusing on forensic evidence to establish the sequence and timing of the killings and are analysing CCTV footage. The bodies were recovered from locations in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Arun Dev Arun Dev is an Assistant Editor with the Karnataka bureau of Hindustan Times. news.headline: 4-year-old boy falls into open sewer manhole in outer Delhi's Ranhola, search-rescue operation on
news.story_lead: 4-year-old boy falls into open sewer manhole in outer Delhi's Ranhola, search-rescue operation on According to the police, the operation is still ongoing to find and rescue the child or retrieve his body, with teams from the DFS, NDRF involved. A four-year-old boy is feared to have died after he fell into an open sewer manhole at Dass Garden Park near Nangli Vihar in outer Delhi’s Ranhola on Tuesday afternoon, after which a multi-agency search and rescue operation was launched. According to the police, the operation is still ongoing to find and rescue the child or retrieve his body, with teams from the Delhi Fire Services, the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), and the local administration involved.
news.full_article_text: 4-year-old boy falls into open sewer manhole in outer Delhi's Ranhola, search-rescue operation on According to the police, the operation is still ongoing to find and rescue the child or retrieve his body, with teams from the DFS, NDRF involved. A four-year-old boy is feared to have died after he fell into an open sewer manhole at Dass Garden Park near Nangli Vihar in outer Delhi’s Ranhola on Tuesday afternoon, after which a multi-agency search and rescue operation was launched. According to the police, the operation is still ongoing to find and rescue the child or retrieve his body, with teams from the Delhi Fire Services, the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), and the local administration involved. The boy’s parents and relatives have remained around the scene, hoping that their son is rescued alive. The boy's father told the media that his son and another boy came to the park to play. “My son went near the sewer and fell into a manhole that was open and died. The rescue teams are telling us that they will find my son. We are poor people; what can we say now,” he said. What the police said Deputy commissioner of police (DCP) for outer areas, Vikram Singh, said that the Ranhola police station received a call on Tuesday at about 3.21pm regarding an incident in which a four-year-old boy fell into a sewer while playing. A team from the police station reached the scene near Kheri Baba Pul, located along the “Ganda Nala” (drain). “There is a sewer line running alongside the service road, next to the drain. The child, a resident of Som Bazar Wali Gali, Mohan Garden, was brought to Das’s Garden Park by his mother. While moving towards the drain, he fell into the sewer manhole,” DCP Singh said. Police said teams from the DFS, the NDRF, and the local administration also arrived at the scene and launched a search-and-rescue operation. “The rescue teams are currently at the scene, working to locate and rescue the child. The boy has not been found/recovered from the sewer so far. Further efforts are being made by the rescue team and NDRF to locate and extract the child from the drain,” DCP Singh said. The police said a case of causing death by negligence has been registered under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) at the Ranhola police station, and an investigation has been initiated to ascertain the exact sequence of events leading to the incident and fix responsibility. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Karn Pratap Singh Karn Pratap Singh has been writing on crime, policing, and issues of safety in Delhi for almost a decade. static_gk: Science 20 (S20) is the official science engagement group of the G20, bringing together national science academies of member countries.
The G20 (Group of Twenty) was established in 1999 as a premier forum for international economic and scientific cooperation.
news.headline: G20 Science Academies Call for AI and Satellite Technology to Strengthen Disaster Response
news.story_lead: The science academies of G20 member countries have advocated for the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and satellite technology to enhance global disaster response capabilities. The proposal highlights the critical role of modern technologies in predicting, monitoring, and mitigating the impacts of natural hazards.
news.full_article_text:
### Integration of AI and Satellite Tech for Disaster Mitigation

Science academies representing the G20 nations have recommended leveraging Artificial Intelligence and space-based technologies to modernize disaster management systems globally.

Key Factual Details:
- **Role of AI**: Artificial Intelligence can process complex environmental data to improve predictive modeling, hazard mapping, and early warning accuracy.
- **Satellite Remote Sensing**: Earth observation satellites provide real-time spatial data essential for tracking severe weather events, assessing structural damage, and coordinating rescue operations.
- **Global Science Cooperation**: The collective call by G20 science academies emphasizes the need for cross-border data sharing and collaborative scientific initiatives to lower disaster risk worldwide.
bullet_points: G20 Science Academies recommended utilizing AI and satellite technology to boost disaster response.
Artificial Intelligence can enhance early warnings and rapid hazard prediction.
Satellite imagery provides real-time situational awareness during natural emergencies.
The initiative supports global scientific collaboration for effective disaster risk reduction.
key_facts: G20 Science Academies issued a joint call for using AI and satellite technology in disaster response.
Focus areas include early warning systems, real-time tracking, and post-disaster damage assessment.
The event was reported on November 11, 2026.
important_dates: 2026-11-11: Recommendation released by G20 Science Academies.
exam_relevance: UPSC Prelims: Role of S20/G20 science forums, application of remote sensing and AI in environmental monitoring.

Integrating satellite remote sensing with AI predictive analytics enables proactive risk management, aligning with global priorities under the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.
causes: Increasing severity and frequency of climate-induced natural disasters globally.
impacts: Improved accuracy in disaster forecasting and faster emergency response coordination.
challenges: Disparities in technological access and data-sharing protocols across developing and developed nations.
constitutional_or_policy_link: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 (Priority 1: Understanding disaster risk using scientific tools).
way_forward: Establish open-access scientific data protocols among G20 nations and build technological capacity in vulnerable regions.

- AI Applications: Predictive modeling, risk assessment, real-time decision support.
- Satellite Applications: Damage assessment, earth observation, emergency communications.
- International Alignment: Aligns with Sendai Framework Priority 1 (Science-based risk understanding).

news.full_article_text: Dipke gets exemption from in-person appearance before magistrate on medical grounds The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Abhijeet Dipke’s counsel cited medical grounds for his absence. Cockroach Janta Party ( CJP ) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been granted an exemption from appearing in-person before the special executive magistrate (SEM) regarding the preventive inquiry against him. The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Dipke’s counsel, Abhik Chimni, cited medical grounds for his absence. The matter has been posted for December 2 for further proceedings. During the proceedings, Chimni was also provided copies of the “kalandra” (preventive police report) and other legal documents that the Delhi Police relied on to issue Dipke a show-cause notice, asking him to furnish a bond for maintaining peace. ALSO READ: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke says he spent night at airport on way back from Kochi protest This development comes weeks after Dipke was granted conditional bail by an SEM following his arrest over an alleged breach of a peace bond he furnished earlier. One principal condition imposed on him was that he must ensure no breach of peace on his part for a period of one year. Dipke was detained on October 16 while heading towards Connaught Place for a protest march called by the CJP under the banner of ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’. The march was called despite a Delhi Police notice asking him not to participate, citing prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). ALSO READ: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke predicts ‘Modi govt’s defeat in 2029’ at anti-SIR rally in Kochi: ‘He will definitely go’ He was subsequently arrested on October 17 for allegedly violating a peace bond furnished on October 10. He was later released on a conditional bail bond by the special executive magistrate. The bond was intended to secure an undertaking from him to maintain peace and prevent any disturbance to public order for a year. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Arnabjit Sur Arnabjit Sur is a Senior Correspondent with Hindustan Times who primarily covers stories from the capital's trial courts. Previously, he has worked for English dailies such as The Hindu, Indian Express and Millennium Post, where he has focused on crime and legal stories, especially incorporating both the subjects into producing long-form investigative work. Known for his penchant for minutely tracking high-profile cases with both city and national relevance, he has broken several chargesheets and police remand papers in his six-year-long career. news.story_lead: Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go home - Published 1 hour ago Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest. There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy. Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
news.full_article_text: Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go home - Published 1 hour ago Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest. There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy. Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund. The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood. Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (Â£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors. Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large. Journalists jostled for a glimpse of Najib as he was driven to his home, which has been declared a federal prison Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday. Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest. Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials. In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal. In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home. The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately. Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home. He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; Â£7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts. Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025 , in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; Â£422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028. news.headline: As Delhi gasps for clean air, pollution in NCR dropped from Parliament panel meeting agenda
news.story_lead: As Delhi gasps for clean air, pollution in NCR dropped from Parliament panel meeting agenda The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned and discuss the issue. As Delhi struggles with polluted air, a Parliamentary committee has decided to drop the key issue of air pollution in NCR from the agenda of its November 17 meeting, prompting a Congress member to raise strong objections with the panel chairperson. The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned on the issue and hold a discussion.
news.full_article_text: As Delhi gasps for clean air, pollution in NCR dropped from Parliament panel meeting agenda The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned and discuss the issue. As Delhi struggles with polluted air, a Parliamentary committee has decided to drop the key issue of air pollution in NCR from the agenda of its November 17 meeting, prompting a Congress member to raise strong objections with the panel chairperson. The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned on the issue and hold a discussion. The panel circulated the agenda for the meeting, which included the air pollution issue, among its members on November 5, but dropped the topic from its revised agenda. Also Read | AQI of 387 in India would be nearly 1,500 in US and 10 in UK. Why the range is so wide Congress member Ajay Maken has raised strong objections to the omission of the air pollution issue and has written to the committee chairperson, Radha Mohan Das Agrawal. Agrawal, when contacted, said he was not aware of the letter by Ajay Maken. "I am ignorant of the letter," he told PTI when asked about Maken's letter to him. On why the pollution issue was dropped in the revised agenda, Agrawal said he does not discuss issues relating to the Committee meetings in public. The earlier agenda for the panel meeting stated, "To hear the views of Ministry of Home Affairs and concerned agencies on the subject 'Air pollution in Delhi-NCR: Enforcement of Regulatory measures, effective implementation of GRAP measures, protection of vulnerable sections and coordination among law enforcement and government agencies." The amended agenda has omitted the air pollution issue and will now only hear the views of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways as well as the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on the issue of "drug trafficking and narcotics control: Emerging threats and institutional response". "I wish to register my objection to the omission of the air-pollution hearing from the revised agenda for 17 November 2026. Given the urgency of the health risks, I request that this change be reconsidered and the hearing restored to that date," Maken said in his letter to Agrawal. "I therefore request restoration of the air-pollution hearing on 17 November. If restoration is not possible, please fix and communicate the earliest firm alternative date, together with the reason for the change. I would be grateful for a response before the scheduled meeting," the Congress MP said. Maken said he had requested examination of air pollution in his letter of November 2 and thanked the committee chairperson for including the subject in its programme for 2026-27, as published in Bulletin Part II dated November 6, No. 66837 as item 13. "The original public notice dated 5 November scheduled the hearing with the Ministry of Home Affairs and concerned agencies for 17 November at 2 p.m. The revised public notice dated 6 November omits that hearing. It gives no reason for this change," he said in his letter to the panel chairperson. Maken demanded that the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs restore its hearing on air pollution. "The official meeting schedule, read at 12:56 IST on 10 November, lists sittings on 16 and 17 November with no air-pollution item on either day, and no new date has been notified," he said. Also Read | High pollution alert issued in London after PM2.5 levels exceed WHO limits by 8 times Maken said Delhi's air-pollution crisis must be treated as a public-health emergency. "A reading of 500 is a ceiling and not the actual reading, because CPCB's index is capped at 500. CPCB's own calculator has severe-band formulas that run on above 500, but a display cap reduces every result above 500 to 500. "A station is held at 500 once its 24-hour PM2.5 passes 380 micrograms per cubic metre, or its 24-hour PM10 passes 510. At a PM2.5 of 600, CPCB's formula gives about 669.2, and the index shows 500," he said. Protection of vulnerable people, effective enforcement and coordination among agencies require urgent attention, he said, adding that these matters are already within the Committee's selected subject. "A prompt hearing would allow the Committee to examine what the responsible agencies are doing, whether implementation is falling short and what immediate corrective action is needed. "Air pollution remains in the published annual programme. My concern is specifically the removal of the scheduled November 17 hearing at a time when these health risks demand timely scrutiny. Its omission requires an explanation and a definite date for examination," he said in his letter to Agrawal.

news.full_article_text: Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on board - Published 10 November 2026, 12:25 GMT Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together. Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension. Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats. Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other. "[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties. He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran". Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments. "I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute." The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months. One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition. On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government. Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office. This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps". Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities. The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do. Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation. The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside. If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs. In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
